extracted.intended_audience: prospective participants and collaborators (Harvard students, technologists, scholars, policymakers, platform leaders, government officials, civil society, and researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the Assembly: Disinformation program at the Berkman Klein Center, its three tracks (Assembly Forum, Assembly Student Fellowship, Assembly Fellowship), participant profiles, activities, and expected outputs for cohorts addressing disinformation in the digital public sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program focus — exploring disinformation in the digital public sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly Program brings together participants from academia, industry, government, and civil society from across disciplines to explore disinformation in the digital public sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assembly explores disinformation from a range of perspectives and addresses challenges and opportunities of public and private sector responses to disinformation and related problems, including within cybersecurity, platforms and internet governance, public health, politics, elections, democracy, and public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-sector collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring together cohorts that include academia, industry, government, and civil society to work across disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program is collaborative by design and builds on existing research and networks; it emphasizes interdisciplinary programming and the Berkman Klein Center's role as a convener and long view on internet problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-track program design
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize programming around three tracks — the Assembly Forum, the Assembly Student Fellowship, and the Assembly Fellowship — designed to bring together cohorts of experts, professionals, and students to better understand and actively address complex disinformation issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each track targets different audiences and modes of engagement (senior leadership discussion, student seminars, practitioner/scholar project work) while building a community of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly Forum — senior leadership discussion forum
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly Forum is a discussion forum for senior leadership from internet platforms, the government (including the U.S. national security community), the academic field, and civil society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Forum hosts high-level briefings with special guests and conversations conducted under the Chatham House Rule on specific challenges and solutions for disinformation; it aims to elicit candid perspectives, surface points of agreement, make progress on hard problems, and offer recommendations where pertinent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum outputs and advisory role
rubrics_metrics.description: Share insights from the Forum through public-facing activities and advisory relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Forum hosts live public events, produces interviews with members (e.g., Berkman Klein Center’s Breakdown), writes on topics of interest, and Forum members also serve as advisors to Assembly Fellows and Student Fellows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student Fellowship — cohort composition and seminar participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly Student Fellowship brings together a cohort of Harvard students from a range of disciplines and schools to participate in problem-oriented seminars led by Harvard faculty, practitioners, and experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student fellows engage in active discussion about disinformation problems in the public interest; seminar topics include disinformation and election security, race and racism, public health, platform policies, and journalism. Fellows become part of an interdisciplinary community learning alongside faculty, staff, Forum members and Assembly Fellows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly Fellowship — non-residential four-month practitioner/scholar fellowship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly Fellowship is a non-residential four-month fellowship for technologists, scholars, and policymakers to tackle difficult problems in technology and policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fellows develop projects and prototypes aimed at addressing challenges related to the year’s theme (e.g., disinformation), with a deep focus on the public interest; after the fellowship, fellows are encouraged to apply learnings to their ongoing work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project and prototype development emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Fellows are expected to develop projects and prototypes that address the program's theme and public-interest challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During 2020–21 the Fellowship invited ongoing projects from prior years to support continued work; returning Fellows both receive support and comprise a continuing community of practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant eligibility and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Different tracks target specific participant types: Forum — senior leadership from platforms/government/academia/civil society; Student Fellowship — Harvard students across disciplines; Assembly Fellowship — technologists, scholars, policymakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracks are designed to bring together relevant expertise for cross-pollination: Forum members advise Fellows and students, student fellows learn alongside practitioners, and fellows build practitioner-focused projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality practice — use of Chatham House Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversations in the Assembly Forum are sometimes conducted under the Chatham House Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to elicit candid perspectives from senior participants and allow frank discussion of challenges and solutions; public-facing reporting of insights happens via separate live events, interviews, and writings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest and interdisciplinary orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize work in the public interest and interdisciplinary approaches to tackling disinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program builds on prior work at the Center on intermediary responsibility, cybersecurity, and the media ecosystem, treating disinformation as an intersectional issue that requires long-term, cross-disciplinary engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outputs and dissemination expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Program activities are expected to produce shareable outputs to inform broader discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of outputs include live public events, interviews (Breakdown series), written pieces, and recommendations that surface from Forum and fellowship discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program staffing, leadership, and administrative support
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear leadership and staff roles support program logistics, research, design, facilitation, and communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership is named (Professor Jonathan Zittrain) and staff roles (program coordinator, staff fellow, senior research coordinator, program design co-lead, assistant research director, senior program manager) are described with responsibilities for facilitation, research support, communications, and program management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding transparency and acknowledgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The program acknowledges its funders and notes changes in support over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current support is from the Ethics and Governance of AI Fund; previous supporters include Craig Newmark Philanthropies, the Knight Foundation, and the William and Flora Hewlett Foundation; more funding information is available via a link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site currency notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the information on this site may be out of date, as it is not updated regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and prospective applicants should verify current program details and timelines, particularly given the program's transition to the Institute for Rebooting Social Media.
